The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)

- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Now the chat-sync script — a PowerShell script that mirrors your Claude conversation + memory between `~/.claude/projects/…` and the repo's `.claude-history/` folder, in either direction:

input.content:
<#
    sync-history.ps1  -  Mirror Claude Code chat + memory into the git repo.

    Claude Code stores this project's conversation transcripts and memory under
        %USERPROFILE%\.claude\projects\<derived-name>\
    where <derived-name> is the project's absolute path with every non
    alphanumeric character replaced by '-'. We mirror that folder into the
    repo's .claude-history\ so the chat travels with the code.

      save     copy  ~/.claude/projects/<derived>/  ->  repo/.claude-history/
      restore  copy  repo/.claude-history/           ->  ~/.claude/projects/<derived>/

    Copies are merge-only (never delete), so nothing is lost if a session
    exists on one machine but not the other. Run 'restore' after pulling on a
    new machine, then use Claude Code's /resume to pick up the conversation.

    NOTE: For 'restore' to land in the right place, launch Claude Code from the
    same absolute path on every machine (e.g. d:\DummyProjects\webgl and
    firebase learning). The derived folder name is computed from that path.
#>
param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
    [ValidateSet('save', 'restore')]
    [string]$Direction
)

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

# Repo root = parent of this .claude folder
$repoRoot  = Split-Path -Parent $PSScriptRoot
$derived   = ($repoRoot -replace '[^a-zA-Z0-9]', '-')
$claudeDir = Join-Path $env:USERPROFILE ".claude\projects\$derived"
$histDir   = Join-Path $repoRoot ".claude-history"

function Copy-Tree($src, $dst) {
    if (-not (Test-Path $src)) { return $false }
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $dst | Out-Null
    $items = Get-ChildItem -Path $src -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    if (-not $items) { return $false }
    foreach ($item in $items) {
        # Skip nothing special; both trees are small (JSONL + memory md files).
        Copy-Item -Path $item.FullName -Destination $dst -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    }
    return $true
}

try {
    if ($Direction -eq 'save') {
        $ok = Copy-Tree $claudeDir $histDir
        if ($ok) { Write-Host "[claude-sync] saved chat -> .claude-history" }
    }
    else {
        $ok = Copy-Tree $histDir $claudeDir
        if ($ok) { Write-Host "[claude-sync] restored chat -> $claudeDir" }
    }
}
catch {
    # Never let a sync hiccup interrupt the Claude session.
    Write-Host "[claude-sync] skipped: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}
exit 0

<#
    sync.ps1  -  One-command sync of code + Claude Code chat between machines.

    Workflow (office <-> home), using the SAME folder path on both machines:

        End of a session:   .\sync.ps1 push      # capture chat, commit, push
        Start on other PC:  .\sync.ps1 pull      # pull, restore chat, then /resume

    'push'  ->  mirror chat into .claude-history, commit everything, push
    'pull'  ->  pull latest, then restore chat into ~/.claude so /resume works

    This is fully manual: nothing is committed or pushed unless you run it.
#>
param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
    [ValidateSet('push', 'pull')]
    [string]$Action
)

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
Set-Location $PSScriptRoot

if ($Action -eq 'push') {
    Write-Host "==> Capturing Claude chat into .claude-history ..."
    & powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File ".\.claude\sync-history.ps1" save

    Write-Host "==> Staging changes ..."
    git add -A

    if (git diff --cached --quiet; $LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) {
        Write-Host "Nothing to commit. Working tree clean."
    }
    else {
        $stamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'
        git commit -m "sync: $stamp"
        Write-Host "==> Pushing ..."
        git push
    }
}
else {
    Write-Host "==> Pulling latest ..."
    git pull
    Write-Host "==> Restoring Claude chat into ~/.claude ..."
    & powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File ".\.claude\sync-history.ps1" restore
    Write-Host ""
    Write-Host "Done. Open Claude Code here and run /resume to continue the conversation."
}

<#
    sync.ps1  -  One-command sync of code + Claude Code chat between machines.

    Workflow (office <-> home), using the SAME folder path on both machines:

        End of a session:   .\sync.ps1 push      # capture chat, commit, push
        Start on other PC:  .\sync.ps1 pull      # pull, restore chat, then /resume

    'push'  ->  mirror chat into .claude-history, commit everything, push
    'pull'  ->  pull latest, then restore chat into ~/.claude so /resume works

    This is fully manual: nothing is committed or pushed unless you run it.
#>
param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
    [ValidateSet('push', 'pull')]
    [string]$Action
)

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
Set-Location $PSScriptRoot

if ($Action -eq 'push') {
    Write-Host "==> Capturing Claude chat into .claude-history ..."
    & powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File ".\.claude\sync-history.ps1" save

    Write-Host "==> Staging changes ..."
    git add -A

    if (git diff --cached --quiet; $LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) {
        Write-Host "Nothing to commit. Working tree clean."
    }
    else {
        $stamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'
        git commit -m "sync: $stamp"
        Write-Host "==> Pushing ..."
        git push
    }
}
else {
    Write-Host "==> Pulling latest ..."
    git pull
    Write-Host "==> Restoring Claude chat into ~/.claude ..."
    & powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File ".\.claude\sync-history.ps1" restore
    Write-Host ""
    Write-Host "Done. Open Claude Code here and run /resume to continue the conversation."
}

> Pick a background → drag & scale stickers/furniture onto it → make several pages → save it → it shows up as a cover-card on the menu → tap a card to flip through the pages read-only.

Think "digital picture-book creator" or "room decorator." That framing drives a lot of the design decisions below. It's almost certainly **2D**, not 3D.

## The one trap that decides pass/fail

**The Firebase Unity SDK does *not* support WebGL builds.** It only targets Android/iOS/desktop. A lot of candidates will import the SDK, build to WebGL, and it silently dies. The title literally says "WebGL / Firebase," so I'm fairly sure this is a deliberate filter.

The clean way through, and a great thing to explain in the handover doc/video:

- **Talk to Firebase over its REST API using `UnityWebRequest`** — Firestore REST for the saved-project data, Firebase Storage download URLs for the remote assets. This runs natively in WebGL with zero plugins.
- Alternative is bridging the **Firebase JS SDK via a `.jslib`** — more powerful (realtime listeners) but much more plumbing. I'd only do that if we specifically want realtime.

My recommendation: **REST for reliability**, and mention the JS-SDK bridge in the doc as the "if we needed realtime" path (shows you know both).

## Caching — they marked this "critical," so it's where you win points

They want your *approach* **and** the *WebGL limitations*. I'd build a **two-tier cache** and be ready to talk about it:

1. **In-memory** `Dictionary<assetId, Sprite>` for the session (instant re-use).
2. **Persistent** across reloads — either lean on the **browser HTTP cache** (Firebase Storage can send `Cache-Control`), or explicitly write decoded bytes to `Application.persistentDataPath` (which in WebGL is **IndexedDB** via Emscripten's IDBFS).

WebGL limitations to name in the writeup (this is the depth they're grading):
- No real filesystem — `persistentDataPath` is IndexedDB, flushed asynchronously (`FS.syncfs`), so there's data-loss risk if you don't sync.
- Browser **storage quotas** + eviction.
- **CORS** — remote assets must return proper headers (Storage does, once configured).
- **Memory ceiling** — big textures blow the WASM heap; you must dispose/manage.
- No `System.IO`, no threads for I/O — everything goes through `UnityWebRequest` coroutines.

## Architecture (they require MVC and/or event-driven — I'd do both)

- **EventBus** — decouples everything (`OnAssetSelected`, `OnObjectPlaced`, `OnPageChanged`, `OnSaveRequested`, `OnProjectLoaded`).
- **Models** — `ProjectModel`(id, title, coverUrl, pages[]) · `PageModel`(backgroundId, placedObjects[]) · `PlacedObjectModel`(assetId, **normalized** pos, scale, rotation, zIndex) · `AssetCatalog`(definitions with id/type/thumbnail/url).
- **Services** — `AssetService` (load+cache) · `PersistenceService` (Firestore/Storage REST) · `SceneCaptureService` (cover thumbnail via RenderTexture→PNG).
- **Controllers** — `MainMenuController`, `EditorController`, `PlaybackController`.
- **Views** — dumb prefabs that only render + raise input events.

Two design choices worth calling out:
- Store objects as **asset references + normalized transforms** (0–1 of a 1920×1080 stage), never raw pixels — that's what makes "scales properly on different screens" basically free with a **CanvasScaler** set to 1920×1080 reference.
- **Cover generation** = snapshot page 1 to a RenderTexture → PNG → upload to Storage (or base64 in the Firestore doc).

## Reality check on scope

This is a genuinely full app, and it's **one of two tasks**, plus a handover doc **and** a 5–10 min video — with **5 days** to 16 July. That's tight but doable if we don't gold-plate. Rough shape:

- **Day 1** — architecture skeleton + event bus + data models + Firebase REST wiring + dynamic asset catalog & asset menu
- **Day 2** — editor: place / drag / scale, background select, pages + nav
- **Day 3** — save/load (Firestore + Storage) + cover thumbnails + Main Menu library
- **Day 4** — playback mode + WebGL build + caching polish + responsive + bugfix
- **Day 5** — Task 2, handover doc, video, deploy live

Nice tie-in: **host the WebGL build on Firebase Hosting** → you get a live link to include in the reply (they asked for live links), and it keeps everything in one Firebase project.

## Before we lock the plan, a few things I want your take on

1. **Firebase approach** — you good with **REST via `UnityWebRequest`** (my rec), or do you want the JS-SDK bridge, or even local-only persistence with Firebase just for assets?
2. **Do you already have a Firebase project / console access?** (Storage + Firestore need to exist and have read rules set.)
3. **2D confirmed?** I'm assuming a 2D Canvas/sprite editor — shout if you pictured 3D.
4. **How much have you got in the tank** — are we going for a polished MVP that nails the core loop + caching story, or full-featured? Given Task 2 + doc + video, I'd steer polished-MVP.

And whenever you can, send over **Task 2 (Search & Content Discovery)** — I can't size the full week until I see it. What's your gut on the approach so far?

Now I've got the full picture. Task 2 is the smaller, sharper one — and importantly, **the two tasks rhyme**, which changes how we should build.

## Task 2 in one line

Pull a messy content library from Firebase **Realtime Database**, robustly parse a junk `CoverInfo` string into **Name / Author / Date**, search by name or author, render result cards — and prove it scales to 10k+.

The two parts they actually grade hard:
1. **Parsing the deliberately-messy string** — they even forbid cleaning the source, so all the mess has to be handled in code.
2. **Search performance + the 10k scalability essay** (explicitly a required section in the doc/video).

## The key realization: both tasks share a spine

| | Task 1 (Editor) | Task 2 (Search) |
|---|---|---|
| Firebase from WebGL | Storage + DB via REST | **RTDB via REST** (`/path.json`) |
| Architecture | MVC + event-driven | MVC + event-driven |
| UI | card grid + pooling | card list + pooling |
| States | loading/error | loading/error |

Both hit the **same Firebase-SDK-doesn't-support-WebGL wall** and both solve it with REST. So we build a **shared `Core`** once (EventBus, `FirebaseRestClient`, pooled card UI, loading/error) and drop two feature scenes on top. That's less work *and* it literally demonstrates the "scalable systems / overall system design" that Task 1 grades.

## The parser (heart of Task 2)

A **config-driven extractor chain**, not brittle `Split()`:

1. **Tokenize** on the mixed separators (`_`, `|`, extras), trim, drop empties.
2. **Classify** tokens through a chain of extractors:
   - `DateExtractor` — multi-format `DateTime.TryParseExact` + regex fallback
   - `AuthorExtractor` — markers ("by", "author:") + heuristics
   - `NameExtractor` — the remainder / most title-like token
3. **Config as data** — separators, date formats, author markers live in a ScriptableObject → tunable, reusable, zero hardcoded IDs.
4. **Null-safe** — missing/malformed → empty, never throws.
5. **Unit-tested** — `com.unity.test-framework` is *already in the project*, so I'll add EditMode tests with a table of nasty inputs. That's your "parsing robustness" score, locked in.

⚠️ One dependency: the exact `CoverInfo` format is unknown until we see the real DB. The parser is adaptive by design, but we tune it once we have access.

## The scalability answer (required section — worth prepping now)

- **Now (1k):** load-all once → parse once → in-memory index → debounced O(n) filter → **pooled** result cards. Trivial at this size.
- **10k+ redesign:** client full-load stops scaling → push search server-side:
  - Cloud Function builds a **derived, normalized index** in a *separate* node (respects "don't modify the source"), **or** pipe into **Algolia/Typesense/Meilisearch** (Firebase's recommended full-text pattern)
  - **parse once at ingestion**, not per-query on the client
  - RTDB **prefix queries** (`orderByChild + startAt/endAt + limitToFirst`) + pagination/infinite scroll
  - client-side: debounce, request cancellation, LRU query cache, UI virtualization

## One thing quietly in your favor

Both docs require you to describe **"use of AI tools and how they supported your work."** So leaning on Claude Code is *expected and scored*, not something to hide — and the git + chat-sync we set up literally records our collaboration. That's ready-made material for that section.

- **Task 1** is the beast — ~3.5 days (editor, caching, save/load, playback)
- **Task 2** is lighter — ~1.5 days (search UI, REST fetch, parser + tests, pooled results, scalability writeup)
- **Docs ×2 + videos ×2 + live deploy** (Firebase Hosting) — ~1 day, overlapped

Tight but very doable, especially with AI assist (which they want anyway).

Good call — let's nail the mental model before any code. Two questions, two clear answers.

# 1) All that loading & saving — how we'll actually do it

The trick that makes this manageable: **we separate the "recipe" from the "ingredients."**

- **Ingredients** = the actual background and sticker **images**. These are the big files. They live in the cloud **once**, and we download + cache them.
- **Recipe** = a tiny text description of a book: *"use background #5; put sticker #12 at position (0.3, 0.6), scaled 1.5×, on page 2."* Just words and numbers. Tiny.

So when the user saves a book, **we do NOT save the images** — they already live in the cloud. We just save the little recipe (plus one cover snapshot). That's why, even though it *looks* like a lot of loading/saving, most of it is tiny text moving around, and the heavy images are downloaded once and reused.

Here's every load/save moment, following a real user:

| Moment | What happens | Load or Save? | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| App opens (home shelf) | Ask cloud: "list my saved books" → get titles + cover links → show covers | **Load** | tiny + small images |
| Click "Create New" | Ask cloud: "what backgrounds/stickers exist?" → get the list → show the picker menu with thumbnails | **Load** | tiny + small thumbnails |
| Pick a background / sticker | Download that full image (or grab from **cache** if seen before) | **Load** | one image (cached after 1st time) |
| Dragging, scaling, adding pages | All happens **in memory** — nothing touches the cloud yet | — | — |
| Hit **Save** | Build the recipe (JSON) → snap a cover picture → upload cover → write recipe to cloud DB | **Save** | tiny recipe + 1 cover |
| Open a saved book (read mode) | Read its recipe → fetch the images it names (mostly from **cache** = instant) → show pages | **Load** | tiny + cached images |

**Where each thing lives:**
- **Images** (backgrounds, stickers, covers) → **Firebase Storage** (a cloud folder for files)
- **The list of available assets** + **the saved book recipes** → **Firebase Database** (cloud text/data)
- **Copies of downloaded images** → **cached in the browser** so we never re-download

So the whole "lots of loading/saving" boils down to: **a handful of small web requests to Firebase, plus images that get cached after the first download.** That's it.

---

# 2) "Firebase REST API" — in plain words

**What is Firebase?** Google's **rent-a-backend**. Instead of you building and running your own server and database, Google hands you ready-made cloud pieces:
- a **Database** (store data),
- **Storage** (store files/images),
- **Hosting** (put your app online).

You just use them; Google runs the machines.

**What's an API?** A way for your app to *talk to* a service — like ordering from a **waiter**. Your app asks ("bring me book #5"), the service brings it back.

**Now the important part — two ways to talk to Firebase:**

**Way A — the SDK (the "special plugin").** Normally in Unity you'd install Firebase's **plugin**: a big bundle of code with nice buttons like `database.GetValue()`.
> ❌ **But this plugin does NOT work in the browser (WebGL).** Google never built it for that. Use it, build to web, it breaks. This is the classic trap in this test.

**Way B — REST (just plain web links). This is what we'll use.**
Every Firebase service is *also* reachable the exact same way your **browser opens a web page** — by visiting a URL and getting text back. "REST API" is just a fancy name for **"talk to it using normal web links."**

The analogy:
- **SDK** = a dedicated **app** with buttons — convenient, but only runs on certain devices.
- **REST** = just **using the website directly** — works anywhere there's internet, including the browser.

What it looks like in practice (don't worry about the syntax, just the idea):
- **Read data** → your app "visits" `https://your-project.firebaseio.com/books.json` → Firebase replies with the data as text. *Literally like opening a link.*
- **Save data** → your app *sends* text **to** that URL → Firebase stores it.
- **Get an image** → Firebase Storage gives every file a normal download link (`https://...`) → you download it like any picture on the web.

And here's why it fits perfectly: Unity has a **built-in tool** for "visit a URL and get the response" called **`UnityWebRequest`** — and it **works great in WebGL**, because it's the same thing the browser already does all day:
- `UnityWebRequest.Get(url)` → read data
- `UnityWebRequest.Put(url, recipe)` → save data
- `UnityWebRequestTexture.GetTexture(url)` → download an image

**One sentence:** *We skip the Firebase plugin entirely and just talk to Firebase over plain web links using Unity's built-in `UnityWebRequest` — which the browser is completely happy with, so nothing breaks in the WebGL build.*

(Small note for later: Firebase decides *who's allowed* to read/write using "rules." For a demo we'll set those to be permissive so it just works — and, tying back to earlier, we keep any secret keys out of the public repo.)

---

Yes — I looked, and now I can tell you exactly what's in there. This is genuinely useful for our task.

## What DragonMouse actually did with Firebase

It uses the **full Firebase Unity SDK** (v13.8.0) — the "special plugin" approach — wired into these manager scripts:

- `FirebaseAuthManager.cs` → **Auth** (login)
- `FirestoreSaveManager.cs` + `PlayerDataManager.cs` → **Firestore** (save/load player data)
- `CloudFunctionManager.cs` → **Cloud Functions**
- `GameAnalytics.cs` → **Analytics**
- `BalanceDataLoader.cs` → loading game-balance data from the cloud
- plus a `google-services.json` config file

And here's the tell: that Firebase folder has libraries for **Android, iOS, and desktop** (`m2repository` = Android, iOS bundles, `x86_64` = desktop) — but **zero WebGL/browser files** (no `.jslib`, no `.wasm`). DragonMouse is an **Android/mobile game**, and that's *why* the SDK worked there.

## The important lesson (this is the whole point)

> **What you did in DragonMouse is exactly what will NOT work here.**

Same Firebase, but a different target:
- **DragonMouse = Android** → the SDK works → you call `FirebaseFirestore.DefaultInstance...` and it just works. ✅
- **This task = WebGL (browser)** → the SDK is dead → you'd import it, build to web, and it breaks. ❌

That's precisely the trap I flagged earlier — and now you've got proof of it sitting in your own project. So for this assessment we **drop the plugin and use REST (plain web links)** instead.

## The good news — a lot carries over

Because you built DragonMouse, you already understand the parts that *do* transfer:
- what a Firebase **project** is, the console, `google-services.json`
- **documents / collections**, saving and loading structured data
- the habit of putting Firebase behind **manager scripts** (`FirestoreSaveManager`, `PlayerDataManager`) — that's already a clean pattern, and we'll do the same here, just with `UnityWebRequest` under the hood instead of the SDK.

Two practical things this tells me:
1. **You already have a Firebase account/console set up.** So for Task 1 you don't start from zero — though I'd spin up a **fresh Firebase project** for the assessment (clean, safe to set open rules, won't touch DragonMouse's live data).
2. One nuance: DragonMouse used **Firestore**, but Task 2 specifically requires **Realtime Database** (a different database inside the same Firebase project). For Task 1 we can use either — I'll pick whichever is cleanest over REST.

---

Want me to open your `FirestoreSaveManager.cs` / `PlayerDataManager.cs` and show you, side by side, **"here's your DragonMouse save code → here's the same thing done the REST/WebGL way"**? That'd make the whole switch click, using code you already wrote.

Great question to ask *now* rather than after setup. Short version: **no Cloud Functions, and no, you won't have to pay.** Let me break it down.

## Cloud Functions — we're not using them

You remembered right: in DragonMouse, **Cloud Functions** is the piece that forced the **paid ("Blaze") plan** — Google makes you put a card on file to use Functions. That's why it felt like "the paid stuff."

**For this assessment we don't need Functions at all.** The only place Cloud Functions came up was in my *Task 2 scalability answer* — "if the library grew to 10,000+ items, you *could* use a Cloud Function to build a search index." That's just something you **describe in the handover doc/video** as "here's how I'd scale it." You **talk about it, you don't build it.** Zero cost.

## Does REST cost money? No.

This is the key thing to understand: **REST vs SDK is not about money — it's just a different door into the *same* Firebase.**

- SDK = walk in through the plugin door
- REST = walk in through the web-link door
- Same house, same rooms, same price (free).

Switching to REST doesn't add any cost. It's literally the same database and storage you'd use anyway.

## What's actually free on Firebase

The free **"Spark" plan** (no card) includes everything the two tasks need:

| Service | We use it for | Free allowance (way more than a demo needs) |
|---|---|---|
| **Realtime Database** | Task 2 library + Task 1 book recipes | ~1 GB stored, 10 GB/month download |
| **Firestore** | (alt for book recipes) | 50K reads/day, 20K writes/day |
| **Hosting** | putting your WebGL build online (live link) | ~10 GB stored, 360 MB/day |
| **Auth** | (only if we bother) | free |

For a demo with a handful of books, you'd use a **fraction of a percent** of these. Nowhere near paying.

## The one honest caveat — and the easy dodge

The *only* thing that might pop up a "add a credit card" prompt is enabling **Firebase Storage** (the image-file service) on a brand-new project — Google recently started routing it through paid Cloud Storage. Two ways we sidestep it completely:

1. **Asset images** (backgrounds/stickers) → host them for **free** on Firebase **Hosting** or even straight from your GitHub repo as plain URLs. They're still "remote assets loaded + cached," which is exactly what the task grades — the grader doesn't care *which* free host.
2. **Cover snapshots** → save the little cover as a tiny text blob (base64) **inside the database** instead of uploading a file. Small thumbnail = a few KB. No Storage needed.

## Bottom line

✅ **No Cloud Functions.**
✅ **REST is free — same services, different door.**
✅ **Both tasks build entirely on the free plan, no credit card** — data in Realtime Database, asset images on a free host, covers as base64, and the live build on Firebase Hosting.

The grader wants to see *remote loading, caching, save/load, and clean architecture* — none of that requires a paid feature.

This is the jackpot. Your `GameBull` folder is a **clean, layered REST SDK for a WebGL game** — exactly the shape we need for the assessment. You've already solved the hard WebGL-networking problems here. Let me lay out what's in it and how directly it maps.

## The architecture (5 layers, each with one job)

| Layer | File | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **Boot** | `GameBullBoot.cs` | Reads config (tokens, ids) from the **page URL** at startup (`Application.absoluteURL` + `[RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod]`). The host webpage injects settings via `?tenantSlug=…&token=…`. |
| **Endpoints** | `GameBullEndpoints.cs` | *One* place for every URL — a base-URL constant + typed builders (`SoloScore()`, `RoomScore(id)`…). Change the server in one spot. |
| **Client** | `GameBullClient.cs` | **The only code that touches the internet.** Two primitives: `GetJson` (read) + `PostJson` (write). Nothing else does networking. |
| **Api** | `GameBullApi.cs` | The "front door": typed methods (`GetContext()`, `SubmitSoloScore()`) + response model classes, parsed with Newtonsoft.Json. The game never sees a URL. |
| **Controller** | `GameBullLobbyController.cs` | The UI (panels, leaderboards) + **downloads remote branding images** and applies them. |

Plus: `Plugins/GameBullClipboard.jslib` (a **WebGL↔browser-JS bridge**), `GameBullApiTester.cs`, and `_backup_old/` (.bak files).

## The WebGL problems you've *already* solved here

These are the exact things the assessment grades — and you have working, battle-tested answers:

1. **Async networking that works in WebGL.** `GameBullClient.SendAsync` wraps Unity's `SendWebRequest()` in a `TaskCompletionSource` so you get clean `async/await` instead of coroutine spaghetti — and it works in single-threaded WebGL.

2. **The WebGL browser-cache gotcha — solved.** Look at `GetJson` (lines 26–36): it appends a unique `_ts=<ticks>-<counter>` to force a fresh fetch, *plus* sets `Cache-Control`/`Pragma: no-cache`, with the comment *"some WebGL browsers ignore no-cache headers but never a unique URL — so do BOTH."* **That's literally the "caching limitations in WebGL" answer Task 1 asks you to explain — from your own experience.** 🔑

3. **Remote image loading — the Task 1 core primitive.** In the LobbyController (lines ~281, 366, 388): `UnityWebRequestTexture.GetTexture(url)` → `DownloadHandlerTexture.GetContent(req)` → `Sprite.Create(...)`, stored in static sprites and applied to the UI/ball/background. That's exactly "load a background/sticker from the internet and show it."

4. **The `.jslib` bridge** (clipboard) — proof you already know how to call browser JavaScript from Unity, which is the fallback path if we ever wanted the Firebase JS SDK.

5. **Config-from-URL** — the browser-app pattern of receiving settings through the page URL.

## How this maps to Task 1 — almost a rename

| GameBull (yours) | Task 1 (book maker) |
|---|---|
| `GameBullClient` (GetJson/PostJson) | `FirebaseClient` — add `PutJson` + a `GetTexture` helper. ~90% reuse. |
| `GameBullEndpoints` | `FirebaseEndpoints` — base DB URL + `Books()`, `Book(id)`, `AssetCatalog()`. |
| `GameBullApi` + model classes | `ContentApi` — `SaveBook`, `LoadBook`, `ListBooks`, `GetAssetCatalog` + `BookModel/PageModel/PlacedObject/AssetDef`. |
| LobbyController's texture download | `AssetService` — download **and cache** sprites. |
| `GameBullBoot` | optional config loader. |

For **Task 2** it's even simpler: same `Client.GetJson` hits the Realtime-DB `.json` URL → `LibraryApi.GetAllContent()` → hand the raw items to the parser.

## The one thing we deliberately *upgrade*

Your GameBull code **cache-busts to force fresh data** — perfect for live scores/lives. But Task 1's assets (backgrounds/stickers) are the **opposite**: immutable, so we want to **cache and reuse**, never re-download.

So the smart design (and a great doc talking point) is: **fresh for data, cached for assets** —
- the **book list** uses your cache-bust trick (always current),
- the **images** go through a new **two-tier cache**: in-memory `Dictionary<assetId, Sprite>` + persistent bytes in IndexedDB (`persistentDataPath`).

That contrast comes straight from reading your existing code — it'll read as real experience, not textbook.

## Bonus: you already have doc templates

There are two markdown guides sitting right there — `GameBull_WebGL_Integration_Guide.md` and `Unity WebGL Game — Complete Setup Guide.md`. Those are ready-made structure for the **Handover Document** deliverable.

Let me save this as a reference so we don't re-derive it later:

I've saved all of this to memory so it carries across sessions/machines.

Yeah — that was the **"Architecture Requirement"** section in both task sheets. It listed **MVC** and **Event-Driven Architecture**. (You said "MVP" — tiny but worth fixing for your doc: the sheet says **MVC**, *Model-View-Controller*. MVP is a close cousin, but use "MVC" so you match their words.) Here's what they mean, plain.

## First — why they even ask

An "architecture pattern" is just **an agreed way to organize your code so it's not one big messy pile.** Like a kitchen where ingredients go in the pantry, cooking happens at the stove, plating at the counter — everyone knows where things live. Without it, code becomes spaghetti where everything touches everything, and fixing one thing breaks five others. The grader wants to see you **don't write one giant script that does everything.**

---

## MVC — think of a restaurant

Three roles, each minding its own business:

- **Model = the kitchen (the data + rules).** It knows *what* the food is — the recipe, the ingredients. In our book-maker: the actual book data (which background, which stickers, their positions), the list of saved books. **Pure data. It doesn't know anything about screens or buttons.**

- **View = the plated dish the customer sees (the screen).** Just presentation — the home shelf, the editor canvas, the sticker menu, the buttons. **It only shows things; it doesn't decide anything.**

- **Controller = the waiter (the coordinator).** Takes the customer's request ("add a sticker"), tells the kitchen (Model) to update, then tells the plating (View) to refresh. **It's the brain in the middle connecting the two.**

The whole point is **separation**: the data doesn't care how it looks, the screen doesn't hold the logic, and the Controller wires them together. So you can redesign the UI without touching the data, or change the data without breaking the UI. And a reviewer instantly knows where to look for what.

> In our app: a `BookModel` (the data) · the editor UI (the View) · an `EditorController` that handles "user dragged a sticker → update the data → refresh the screen."

---

## Event-Driven — think of a dinner bell

Instead of every part of the app **directly calling** every other part, one part just **announces** that something happened, and whoever cares listens and reacts.

**The messy way (direct calls):** when the user hits Save, the Save code personally calls `homeShelf.AddCover()`, then `soundManager.Play()`, then `analytics.Log()`. Now Save is tangled up with everyone — and adding a confetti animation means editing the Save code *again*.

**The clean way (events):** the Save code just rings a bell — **"BookSaved!"** — and doesn't care who's listening. Then:
- the home shelf hears it → adds a new cover,
- a sound effect plays,
- the analytics logger notes it,

…all **without the Save code knowing any of them exist.** Want to add confetti later? Just have the confetti listen for the bell. You never touch Save.

> Analogy: direct calls = you personally phone each friend to say dinner's ready (you must know every number; new friend = update your list). Events = you ring the dinner bell; whoever's hungry comes (you don't know or care who's listening).

In Unity this is just **C# events / `Action`s** or a small **EventBus** — you've almost certainly used these already; this is just the *name* for it.

---

## How they team up

- **MVC** organizes the **big pieces** (data vs screen vs coordinator).
- **Event-driven** is the **communication style** between those pieces — they announce instead of directly wiring into each other.
- Together = tidy, flexible, easy to extend. Which is *exactly* what "structure scalable systems" and "overall system design" are scoring.

---

**Why it's worth points:** in your handover doc/video you literally get to say *"I used **MVC** to separate data / UI / logic, and an **event bus** so parts stay decoupled"* — and then show it. That single sentence + clean folders hits the "code architecture" and "system design" criteria in both tasks.

Want me to show how this looks as **actual folders/scripts** for the book-maker (Model/View/Controller + a few example events), still keeping it simple?

You're right, and it's a good instinct — **architecture first.** One nuance: the data shape *is* part of the architecture (it's the "M/Model" layer), so the clean order is: draw the **skeleton** first, then zoom into the **Model** (data shape), then wire it to **Firebase**. Let's go in your order.

---

# 1) Folder / architecture — the skeleton (mirrors GameBull)

Same layered idea as your GameBull SDK, just organized into MVC. Plain-English job next to each:

```
Assets/
  _Project/                         ← all OUR code (kept separate from imported packages)
    Core/                           ← reusable foundation  (= your GameBull "SDK" layer)
      Net/
        FirebaseClient.cs           ← the ONLY code that touches the internet   (= GameBullClient)
        FirebaseEndpoints.cs        ← every Firebase URL in one place           (= GameBullEndpoints)
      Events/
        EventBus.cs                 ← the "dinner bell" (publish / subscribe)
        AppEvents.cs                ← the list of events (BookSaved, AssetSelected, PageChanged…)
      Assets/
        AssetService.cs             ← download an image + hand back a Sprite
        AssetCache.cs               ← the two-tier cache (memory + browser IndexedDB)
      UI/
        CardView.cs                 ← one reusable "cover card" (shelf now, search later)
        ObjectPool.cs               ← reuse card objects instead of making thousands
        LoadingOverlay.cs           ← the loading / error spinner
    Models/                         ← the DATA — the "M" in MVC (plain C# classes, no Unity)
        BookModel.cs
        PageModel.cs
        PlacedObjectModel.cs
        AssetDefinition.cs
    Services/                       ← app-level "front door"  (= your GameBullApi)
        ContentApi.cs               ← SaveBook / LoadBook / ListBooks / GetCatalog
        ThumbnailService.cs         ← snapshot a page → tiny cover image
    Features/                       ← the screens, each split View + Controller (MVC)
      MainMenu/                     ← the home shelf
        MainMenuController.cs       ← the "C": logic/coordination
        MainMenuView.cs             ← the "V": just shows cards + buttons
      Editor/                       ← create mode
        EditorController.cs
        EditorView.cs
        PlaceableObject.cs          ← drag + scale behaviour on one sticker
        AssetMenuView.cs            ← the picker menu
      Playback/                     ← read-only view mode
        PlaybackController.cs
        PlaybackView.cs
    App/
        AppBootstrap.cs             ← startup: wire the EventBus, load catalog, show menu
  Scenes/
        Main.unity                  ← one scene; panels swap between the 3 features
```

**How to read it (the mental model):**
- **`Core/`** = your GameBull SDK, generalized. `FirebaseClient` ≈ `GameBullClient`, `FirebaseEndpoints` ≈ `GameBullEndpoints`. Built once, reused by everything (and by Task 2 later).
- **`Models/`** = pure data (the book recipe). Knows nothing about screens.
- **`Services/ContentApi`** = the typed "front door" (≈ `GameBullApi`) — the app calls `SaveBook(...)`, never a URL.
- **`Features/`** = each screen as a **View** (shows stuff) + **Controller** (decides stuff). This is where your one giant `GameBullLobbyController` gets split into tidy MVC pieces.
- **`Events/EventBus`** = the dinner bell so those pieces don't wire into each other directly.

> Optional polish (great for the "system design" score): give `Core`, `Models`, and each Feature its own **assembly definition (.asmdef)**. It enforces the boundaries (Core literally *can't* depend on a Feature) and speeds up compiles. We can add these or skip — your call.

---

# 2) Data shape — what a saved book literally is

A saved book is just a small **recipe** (references + numbers), never the actual images:

```json
{
  "id": "book_ab12cd",
  "title": "My Room",
  "createdAt": "2026-07-12T10:30:00Z",
  "updatedAt": "2026-07-12T10:45:00Z",
  "coverBase64": "data:image/jpeg;base64,/9j/4AAQSkZJRg…",   // tiny snapshot, stored inline
  "pages": [
    {
      "backgroundId": "bg_livingroom",
      "objects": [
        { "assetId": "furn_sofa", "x": 0.30, "y": 0.55, "scale": 1.2, "rotation": 0,  "z": 0 },
        { "assetId": "furn_lamp", "x": 0.72, "y": 0.40, "scale": 0.8, "rotation": 15, "z": 1 }
      ]
    },
    {
      "backgroundId": "bg_garden",
      "objects": [
        { "assetId": "furn_tree", "x": 0.50, "y": 0.60, "scale": 1.5, "rotation": 0, "z": 0 }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**The four decisions baked in here (each is a talking point for your doc):**
- **`x`/`y`/`scale` are normalized `0..1`, not pixels** → replays correctly on any screen size. That's how you get "scales properly on different screens" almost for free.
- **`assetId` / `backgroundId` are *references*, not images** → the recipe stays tiny; images live in the cloud + cache.
- **`coverBase64` is stored inline** (a few KB) → no Firebase Storage, no billing (from our cost chat).
- **`z`** = draw order (which sticker sits on top).

These map straight to your `Models/` classes: `BookModel → PageModel[] → PlacedObjectModel[]`.

### How it sits in Firebase (Realtime DB = one big JSON tree)

```
your-db-root
├── assetCatalog                         ← the "ingredients menu" (what users can pick)
│   ├── backgrounds
│   │   ├── bg_livingroom: { "name": "Living Room", "url": "https://…/living.png" }
│   │   └── bg_garden:     { "name": "Garden",      "url": "https://…/garden.png" }
│   └── objects
│       ├── furn_sofa: { "name": "Sofa", "url": "https://…/sofa.png" }
│       └── furn_lamp: { "name": "Lamp", "url": "https://…/lamp.png" }
└── books                                ← every saved book, keyed by id
    ├── book_ab12cd: { …the recipe above… }
    └── book_ef34gh: { … }
```

And because it's just a tree, **each path is a URL** your `FirebaseClient` hits (ties back to the REST talk):

| Action | REST call |
|---|---|
| List all books (for the shelf) | `GET  …/books.json` |
| Open one book | `GET  …/books/book_ab12cd.json` |
| Save a book | `PUT  …/books/book_ab12cd.json` + the recipe |
| Load the picker menu | `GET  …/assetCatalog.json` |

(The `url` values point to the actual images, hosted free on Firebase Hosting or GitHub — no Storage needed.)

Sure — Group A is just **the data**, and the trick to "getting" it is one idea:

> **Each class is one `{ }` block of that JSON you saw. A `List<>` is just a `[ ]` (many of them).**

When we save, C# turns these objects into JSON text. When we load, we turn the JSON text back into these objects. That's literally all "the recipe" is.

## The nesting (like Russian dolls)

```
BookModel  (the whole book)
  └── pages: List<PageModel>          ← a book has MANY pages
        └── objects: List<PlacedObjectModel>   ← a page has MANY stickers
```

A **book** holds **pages**, each page holds **stickers**. That's the entire structure.

## Class by class, mapped to the JSON

**`PlacedObjectModel`** = one sticker. This JSON:
```json
{ "assetId": "furn_sofa", "x": 0.30, "y": 0.55, "scale": 1.2, "rotation": 0, "z": 0 }
```
| field | plain meaning |
|---|---|
| `assetId` | *which* sticker — a name tag ("furn_sofa"), not the image itself |
| `x`, `y` | where on the page, as a **fraction**: `0.30` = 30% from the left, `0.55` = 55% up |
| `scale` | how big (`1` = normal, `1.2` = 20% bigger) |
| `rotation` | tilt, in degrees |
| `z` | who's on top when they overlap (higher = front) |

**`PageModel`** = one page:
```json
{ "backgroundId": "bg_livingroom", "objects": [ …stickers… ] }
```
- `backgroundId` — which background image
- `objects` — the **list** of stickers on this page (`[ ]` = `List<PlacedObjectModel>`)

**`BookModel`** = the whole book:
```json
{ "id": "book_ab12cd", "title": "My Room", "coverBase64": "…", "pages": [ …pages… ] }
```
- `id` — a unique name for this book (so we can find it: `/books/book_ab12cd`)
- `title` — what it's called on the shelf
- `createdAt` / `updatedAt` — timestamps (to sort the shelf)
- `coverBase64` — the little cover picture, stored **as text** (so we skip paid Storage)
- `pages` — the **list** of pages (`List<PageModel>`)

## The odd one out — `AssetDefinition`

This one is **not part of a saved book.** It describes an *available ingredient* — one background or sticker sitting in the catalog (the picker menu):
```json
{ "id": "furn_sofa", "name": "Sofa", "url": "https://…/sofa.png" }
```

Here's how it connects: a saved book only stores the **id** (`"furn_sofa"`). To actually *draw* that sticker, we look up its `id` in the catalog → find its `url` → download the image. So `AssetDefinition` is the **bridge from a name-tag → a real image**.

```
book says:  assetId = "furn_sofa"
                 │
                 ▼   (look it up in the catalog)
AssetDefinition:  id="furn_sofa", url="https://…/sofa.png"
                 │
                 ▼   (download that url, cache it)
             the actual sofa image on screen
```

## Why these two choices (the clever bits)

- **Positions are fractions (0–1), not pixels** → the book replays correctly whether the screen is big or small.
- **Books store IDs, not images** → the recipe stays tiny (just text + numbers); the heavy images live in the cloud and get cached once.

---

content.text:
That's a genuinely sharp question — and it's *exactly* the "performance & scalability" thinking the assessment grades. Let me split it, because there are actually **two different "costs"** hiding in that one line, and they're very different:

## Cost 1 — the *lookup* (id → url). This is basically free.

We do **not** scan through the catalog one-by-one. We load the catalog **once**, and store it in a **Dictionary** (a lookup table keyed by id). A dictionary doesn't search — it **teleports** straight to the entry.

> Analogy: finding a word in a dictionary/index vs. reading every page. `catalog["furn_sofa"]` jumps right to it whether the catalog has 10 items or 100,000. Same instant speed.

Also — the catalog is *small*. It's the **menu of available art** the app ships with (dozens, maybe a few hundred stickers), not per-kid data. One small fetch, once, then instant lookups forever. So "going through a lot of data" never actually happens here.

## Cost 2 — the *download* (the image itself). This is the only slow bit — and the cache kills it.

Downloading `sofa.png` over the internet takes a moment. So we do it **once**, then keep it:

- **First time** we need the sofa → download it, put it in the cache.
- **Every time after** → instant, straight from cache. Same sofa on page 2, in another book, or next week — never re-downloaded.

And the cache dedupes: a 3-page book might have 20 stickers placed but only ~8 *unique* images — so it downloads ~8 things the first time, then replays with **zero** downloads.

You nailed it with "unless it's in local cache?" — yes, that's precisely the design, and it's what Task 1 marks as **"critical."**

## Now — "how about 8000 kids?" 🎯

The key is that our data splits into **two kinds that scale completely differently:**

**① Shared stuff (the catalog + the sticker images)** — *one copy for everyone.*
8000 kids all use the same `sofa.png`. It does **not** multiply with users. Serve it from a **CDN** (Firebase Hosting *is* a global CDN), and each kid's browser caches its own copy. So 8000 kids is no harder than 1 — shared art doesn't grow with the crowd.

**② Per-kid stuff (each kid's saved books)** — *this grows, but each kid only ever touches their own slice.*
Store books under the owner: `/books/{kidId}/…`. When a kid opens the app, we fetch **only their books** (a handful), never all 8000 kids' books. Recipes are tiny text, so even millions of them are cheap when you only pull the few a kid needs.

> Analogy: everyone shares the same **supply cupboard** (art), but each kid opens only **their own drawer** (their books) — never the whole filing cabinet.

## The honest "where it would strain" (this IS the doc answer)

The naïve version breaks at scale, and knowing the fix is what scores points:

| Naïve (breaks) | Scalable fix |
|---|---|
| `GET /books.json` (ALL books) for the shelf | Fetch only `/books/{kidId}` — one kid's slice |
| Load a kid's 1000 books at once | **Paginate** — 20 at a time / infinite scroll |
| Search "books by author" over everything | Add an **index / search service** *(literally Task 2!)* |
| Every kid re-downloads images | **CDN + local cache** (what we're building) |

So the short answer to your worry: the **lookup** is instant (dictionary, not scanning), the **download** happens once then it's cached, and **8000 kids** works because shared art is one cached copy for all, while each kid only ever loads their own small slice.

This reasoning goes almost word-for-word into your **handover doc's performance section** — so that instinct you just had is worth real marks.

Want me to roll into **slice 2 (`ContentApi`)** now, or is there more you want to poke at here first?
or in this case we will use kid id, so that we simple jump to that id in data basea nd pics up its books and info .

Exactly right — you've got it. The kid's id becomes **part of the URL path**, and the database jumps straight to that branch and hands back only that slice. Nobody else's data is even touched.

Concretely, the books tree looks like:
```
books
├── kid_017 : { …their books… }
├── kid_042 : { …their books… }   ← we want this one
└── kid_918 : { …their books… }
```

And the request is literally:
```
GET  https://…firebaseio.com/books/kid_042.json
```

Because Realtime DB is a **tree of folders**, the path `books → kid_042` navigates straight there (keys are indexed), so it's **instant whether there are 5 kids or 80,000** — and it returns *only* kid_042's books + info, never the rest. That's the "open your own drawer, not the whole cabinet" from before, now made real as a URL.

**One practical note so we keep scope sane:**

- In a **real product**, each kid's id comes from **login** (Firebase Auth gives every kid a unique id → we use it as the path). That's the version that scales to 8000 kids.
- For the **assessment demo**, the task doesn't ask for a login system — so we can use a **single placeholder id** (like `"demo"`) and put everything under `/books/demo/…`. Same structure, zero login code to build in 5 days.

So we **build it per-kid-ready** (great for your scalability story in the doc), but **run it with one demo id** to stay realistic for the deadline. Best of both — you get the scalable design to talk about, without burning days on auth.

We'd update `FirebaseEndpoints` slightly so the book paths include the kid id:
```
/books/{kidId}.json          ← that kid's whole shelf
/books/{kidId}/{bookId}.json ← one specific book
```

That's a tiny change I'll fold into **slice 2 (`ContentApi`)** when we wire up Save/Load/List.

content.text:
✅ **Slice 2 is in.** This is the **`ContentApi`** — the "front door." From now on, the app never touches URLs or JSON; it just calls four plain methods:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GetCatalog()` | reads the picker menu (backgrounds + stickers) from Firebase |
| `ListBooks(kidId)` | gets **that kid's** books for the shelf |
| `LoadBook(kidId, bookId)` | opens one full book (to view or edit) |
| `SaveBook(kidId, book)` | saves or overwrites a book (auto-makes its id + timestamps on first save) |

**How it flows** (this is the whole save/load loop, finally wired):
- **Saving** → `SaveBook` turns your `BookModel` into JSON text → hands it to `FirebaseClient.PutJson` → it lands at `/books/{kidId}/{bookId}.json`.
- **Loading** → `GetJson` pulls the text back → turns it into `BookModel`/`AssetCatalog` objects for the app to use.

So it sits exactly on top of what we built in slice 1: **`ContentApi` (front door) → `FirebaseClient` (the internet) → `Models` (the data)**. Same three-layer shape as your GameBull `Api → Client → models`.

**Three small things I did along the way:**
1. **Added Newtonsoft JSON** — Firebase returns data *keyed by id* (like `{ "book_ab12cd": {…} }`), and Unity's built-in JSON can't read those dynamic keys. Newtonsoft can. (Same library your basketball project uses.)
2. **Per-kid paths** — updated `FirebaseEndpoints` so books live at `/books/{kidId}/…`, matching our "each kid opens their own drawer" plan.
3. **Safe parsing** — every read is wrapped so bad/empty data returns an empty result instead of crashing.

⚠️ **Heads up for when you next open Unity:** it'll download the Newtonsoft package (needs internet, takes a few seconds), then everything compiles. Nothing *runs* yet because there's still no screen and no real Firebase URL — but the entire **save/load brain is now done**.

---

**Slice 3 options** — your pick:
- **`AssetService` + caching** — the "download once, reuse" image layer (the part Task 1 marks *critical*). Pure code, no Unity Editor needed.
- **Set up the real Firebase project** now, paste the URL in, and prove Save/Load actually works end-to-end with a tiny tester (like your `GameBullApiTester`) — very satisfying to see it work for real.

Which way — keep coding the cache, or go make it real against Firebase?

in slice 2 you created classes that will have function , that wil ldo the job  ,like waiter , taking food from kitchen to customer . right. and secnondly you added kids id, is ther any mentioning of kid id? in assignemnt, we just disccued that and you answerd this

Two good questions — and the second one is a *really* good catch. Let me be straight on both.

## 1) The "waiter" idea — yes, basically right

`ContentApi` is exactly that: a class whose **functions do the actual job** of fetching/storing data, so the rest of the app doesn't have to. Let me just tidy the restaurant metaphor so the pieces stay straight:

| Piece | Restaurant role |
|---|---|
| **Firebase** (the cloud DB) | the **warehouse/pantry** where all the food is stored |
| **`FirebaseClient`** | the **delivery driver** — the only one allowed to drive to the warehouse |
| **`ContentApi`** | the **order window** — you say "save this book" / "get this kid's books," it deals with the driver and hands you back a clean result |
| **Controller** (we build later) | the **waiter** — talks to the customer (the screen) and places orders at the window |

So you're right that it "carries food" — just note the true *waiter* (Controller) comes later; `ContentApi` is the order window it talks to. Your instinct is correct.

## 2) Is "kid id" in the assignment? — No. Honest answer.

**It is not mentioned anywhere in the task sheets.** There's no login, no users, no accounts, no "kid id" in either Task 1 or Task 2. 

It came **purely from our conversation** — when *you* asked "how about 8000 kids?", I ran with it into the design. So that's on me to flag clearly: it's an addition, not a requirement. Good catch questioning it.

Now — should we keep it? Here's the honest trade-off:

**Keep it (as a single `"demo"` id):**
- Costs almost nothing — the data just gets one extra folder level: `/books/demo/…`
- **No login to build** — we hardcode one id.

✅ **Slice 3 is in** — and this is your *critical* scoring item. Here's the whole thing in plain words.

## The problem

Images are heavy, and downloading over the internet is slow. If a kid puts the same sofa on 5 pages, or reopens their book tomorrow, we do **not** want to re-download that sofa 5 times. So we keep copies close by. That "keep a copy close by" is what a **cache** is.

## The idea: two drawers 🗄️

Think of it like keeping snacks instead of walking to the shop every time. We have **two drawers**:

| Drawer | Speed | Lasts? | = in code |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Memory** | instant ⚡ | only while the app is open | `_memory` dictionary |
| **Disk** | fast | survives closing/reopening the tab | a file in browser storage |

## What happens when the app asks for an image

`AssetService.GetSprite(url)` checks the drawers **in order**, cheapest first:

```
1. In the memory drawer?   → hand it over instantly.           (no internet)
2. In the disk drawer?      → read it, done.                    (no internet)
3. Neither?                 → download it ONCE,
                              then drop a copy in BOTH drawers.  (internet, one time)
```

So the **first** time a sofa is needed → one download. **Every time after that** — same page, another book, or next week — it comes straight from a drawer. Zero re-downloads.

## The clever little extra: "make one pot of coffee"

If two parts of the screen ask for the *same* sofa at the *exact same moment*, we don't start two downloads. The first request starts it; the second one just **waits for that same one** to finish. (That's the `_inFlight` dictionary — "this is already being fetched, join it.") Like: two people ask for coffee at once → you make **one** pot, not two.

## The WebGL limitations — this IS your doc answer 📝

Task 1 says *"explain your caching approach **and** any limitations in WebGL."* You've now got both. The limitations to write down:

1. **The "disk" isn't a real disk.** In a browser there are no files — Unity fakes it on top of the browser's **IndexedDB**, and it saves a little *lazily* (it flushes now and then). So if the tab closes the instant after a download, that disk copy might not have been written yet. (Memory drawer is unaffected — it's just gone on close, which is expected.)
2. **Storage has limits.** The browser caps how much a site can store and can **evict** it if space runs low — so the disk drawer isn't guaranteed forever.
3. **Memory has a ceiling.** WebGL runs in a limited memory box; keeping too many big images in the memory drawer can run the tab out of memory. (For a demo with a handful of assets, fine — at scale you'd add eviction.)
4. **No background threads.** Everything downloads through `UnityWebRequest` on the single browser thread — which is exactly why the "download once" caching matters so much for smoothness.

That numbered list, plus the two-drawer diagram, is a ready-made section for your handover doc and video. 🎯

Great questions — and this is *exactly* the stuff that goes in your "WebGL caching limitations" section, so let's nail it. Plain words.

## What is IndexedDB?

It's a **mini-database built into every web browser** that lets a website stash data **on your computer** — tucked inside the browser, tied to that one website. It survives you closing and reopening the browser.

> Think of it as a **private storage locker the browser gives each website.** Your site gets its own locker; other sites can't see it; and it can hold real files (images), not just tiny text.

There are a few browser-storage options, from tiny to big:
- **Cookies** — tiny (a few KB), text only.
- **localStorage** — small (~5 MB), text only.
- **IndexedDB** — **big, and can hold binary files** (images) → this is the one Unity uses.

When our Unity code writes a cached image to `persistentDataPath`, there are no real files in a browser — so Unity quietly puts it in **IndexedDB**. That's the "disk drawer" from before.

## Does every webpage use it?

The *ability* is in every modern browser, but **each site chooses whether to use it.** Gmail, Google Docs offline, YouTube, and most browser games use it. A simple blog might not. **Our Unity WebGL app does** (automatically, via `persistentDataPath`).

## Limitations

1. **Per-browser + per-site.** Data saved in Chrome isn't in Firefox; another website can't touch it; it doesn't sync across devices. (That's why a new browser re-downloads.)
2. **There's a size limit (quota).** Not unlimited — the browser caps how much your site can store (often a chunk of free disk, sometimes GBs, but **not guaranteed** and it varies by browser/device).
3. **The browser can delete it (eviction).** By default it's "best-effort" storage — if the disk gets full, the browser can **automatically wipe** your site's cache to reclaim space.
4. **Write is a bit lazy.** In WebGL, Unity flushes to IndexedDB periodically — so a copy might not be saved if the tab closes the very instant after a download.

## When does it get erased?

- The user **clears browsing data** / site data / cache.
- **Incognito / private window** — wiped when the window closes.
- The browser **evicts** it under low-disk pressure.
- Some browsers auto-clear storage for sites **not visited in a long time** (e.g., Safari ~7 days).
- Your own code deletes it (if we add a cleanup policy).

👉 It does **not** get erased just from closing the tab normally — that only clears the *memory* drawer. IndexedDB persists across normal closes.

## Your 50,000-pics scenario — the important one 🎯

Here's the key mindset shift:

> **IndexedDB is a *cache* (a convenience copy), not the *warehouse*.**

So with 50,000 images used by many students:

- You **don't** store all 50,000 in IndexedDB. The **cloud + CDN is the warehouse** (the real, always-available copy). IndexedDB only holds the **handful each student recently looked at** — because it's on-demand.
- Even so, a student who browses thousands of images could fill the locker → then the browser **evicts** old ones (or writes start failing at the quota).
- That's **fine** — if a cached pic gets evicted, we just **re-download it from the CDN** (fast). Nothing breaks; it's a cache miss, not data loss.

> Fridge vs. grocery store: IndexedDB is your **fridge** — holds what you're using now, limited space, old stuff gets tossed. The cloud/CDN is the **grocery store** — has everything, always restockable. You never try to fit the whole store in your fridge.

**The scalable design (great for your doc):**
- **Warehouse** = Firebase Storage / CDN (all 50,000, permanent).
- **Fridge** = IndexedDB, holds only a recently-used subset per browser.
- Add our own **"keep newest, toss oldest" (LRU) limit** — e.g., cap the cache at some MB — so we never blow the quota and never rely on it being permanent.
- A cache miss (evicted, or new browser) just re-downloads from the CDN — cheap and fast.

So: yes, they get stored in IndexedDB, but only the **recently-used slice**, and they get erased by **eviction / user-clear / incognito / quota** — which is *okay*, because the cloud is always the real source.

# Task 1 — Interactive Content Creation (WebGL / Firebase)
### Handover Document — DRAFT (living notes, updated as we build)

> Sections below map to Adeeb's required deliverable checklist, so this doc grows
> into the final handover writeup + video script.
>
> **Build status:** engine done (slices 1–3: data models, Firebase REST client,
> save/load API, image caching). Pending: UI (Main Menu / Editor / Playback),
> WebGL build, live deploy.

---

## 1. Overview

A browser-based **"book maker" for kids**:

- **Main Menu** — a shelf of saved books shown as cover-cards, plus a "Create New" button.
- **Create/Editor** — pick a background, add stickers/furniture, drag + scale them, add multiple pages, save.
- **Save** — auto-generates a cover snapshot; the book appears on the shelf.
- **Playback** — tap a cover to flip through the pages read-only.

Runs as a **Unity WebGL** build, designed for **1920×1080**, scaling to any screen.
Data and assets come from **Firebase**, accessed over **REST** (see §3).

## 2. Architecture (MVC + Event-Driven)

Clean, layered structure (mirrors a proven REST-in-WebGL pattern we already had working):

- **Core/Net** — `FirebaseClient` (the ONLY code that touches the internet: `GetJson` / `PutJson` / `GetBytes`) + `FirebaseEndpoints` (every URL in one place).
- **Core/Assets** — `AssetService` (two-tier image cache).
- **Models** — `BookModel → PageModel → PlacedObjectModel`, plus `AssetCatalog` / `AssetDefinition`. Pure data (the "M").
- **Services** — `ContentApi` (typed front door: `Save` / `Load` / `List` / `Catalog`).
- **Features** — `MainMenu` / `Editor` / `Playback`, each split into **View** (shows) + **Controller** (decides).
- **Events** — an `EventBus` so parts announce instead of calling each other directly.

**Why MVC:** separates data / screen / logic, so one can change without breaking the others.
**Why event-driven:** parts announce events ("BookSaved") instead of wiring into each other → decoupled and easy to extend.

## 3. Firebase in WebGL — the key decision

- The **Firebase Unity SDK does NOT support WebGL** (only Android / iOS / desktop). Using it would silently break the browser build.
- **Solution:** talk to Firebase over its **REST API** using `UnityWebRequest` — works natively in WebGL, no plugins.
  - Realtime Database: `GET` / `PUT` on `https://<db>.firebaseio.com/<path>.json`
  - Images: hosted on a free host / CDN, downloaded via `UnityWebRequest`.
- Networking is wrapped as `async/await` via `TaskCompletionSource` (works fine in single-threaded WebGL).

## 4. Data model — the "recipe"

A saved book stores **references + numbers, never images**:

```json
{
  "id": "book_ab12cd",
  "title": "My Room",
  "createdAt": "2026-07-12T10:30:00Z",
  "updatedAt": "2026-07-12T10:45:00Z",
  "coverBase64": "data:image/jpeg;base64,...",
  "pages": [
    { "backgroundId": "bg_livingroom",
      "objects": [
        { "assetId": "furn_sofa", "x": 0.30, "y": 0.55, "scale": 1.2, "rotation": 0, "z": 0 }
      ] }
  ]
}
```

Design choices baked in:
- **Positions normalized 0..1**, not pixels → replays correctly on any screen size.
- **`assetId` references**, not images → recipe stays tiny; images cached separately.
- **`coverBase64` stored inline** → avoids paid Firebase Storage.

Sits in Realtime DB as a tree: `/assetCatalog` (the picker menu) and `/books/{kidId}/{bookId}` (per-kid).

## 5. Asset loading & caching (marked CRITICAL)

- **On-demand:** an image downloads only when first shown — not all upfront.
- **Two-tier cache** (`AssetService`):
  - **Memory** (Dictionary) — instant reuse this session; lost on close.
  - **Disk** (IndexedDB via `persistentDataPath`) — survives reloads; per-browser.
- **Flow:** check memory → check disk → download, then save into both.
- **In-flight de-dupe:** the same url requested twice at once shares ONE download.

## 6. WebGL / IndexedDB limitations (required explanation)

- `persistentDataPath` isn't a real disk in a browser — it's **IndexedDB**, flushed lazily → a copy may be lost if the tab closes the instant after a download.
- **Per-browser + per-site** — not shared across browsers/devices → a new browser re-downloads.
- **Quota limits;** the browser can **evict** under low-disk pressure; the user can clear it; **incognito** wipes on close; some browsers clear storage for sites unvisited for a while.
- **Memory ceiling** in WebGL — too many big textures can run the tab out of memory → needs eviction at scale.
- **No background threads** — all downloads on one thread → caching is what keeps it smooth.

## 7. Scalability thinking (feeds Task 2's required section too)

- **Data splits two ways:** *shared* (catalog + images — one copy for everyone, CDN-served, doesn't grow with users) vs *per-kid* (each kid loads only their own books via `/books/{kidId}`).
- **8000 kids:** shared art is one cached copy for all; each kid pulls only their slice; recipes are tiny text.
- **50,000 images:** IndexedDB is a **cache (fridge)**, not the **warehouse (cloud/CDN)**. Only the recently-used subset is cached; evicted items simply re-download. Add an **LRU cap** so we never blow the quota.
- **Redesign at scale:** fetch only `/books/{kidId}`; **paginate**; add an **index / search service** for discovery; rely on **CDN + browser cache** for images.
- Analogy: IndexedDB = your **fridge** (what you're using now, limited, old stuff tossed); cloud/CDN = the **grocery store** (has everything, always restockable). Never fit the store in the fridge.

## 8. Key decisions & challenges

- **REST over the SDK** (the WebGL blocker).
- **Fresh-for-data, cached-for-assets** — cache-bust the book list (always current); cache the immutable images.
- **`coverBase64`** to stay off paid Storage.
- **Per-kid data with a single `demo` id** — no login to build, but structured to scale.
- **Free Spark plan; no Cloud Functions** (see §10).

## 9. Use of AI tools

See [ai-usage-log.md](ai-usage-log.md).

## 10. Cost

Entire app runs on Firebase's **free (Spark) plan** — Realtime DB free tier, images on a free host/Hosting, covers as base64, the WebGL build on Firebase Hosting. **No credit card, no Cloud Functions.**

- **`assetId` references**, not images → recipe stays tiny; images cached separately.
- **`coverBase64` stored inline** → avoids paid Firebase Storage.

Sits in Realtime DB as a tree: `/assetCatalog` (the picker menu) and `/books/{kidId}/{bookId}` (per-kid).

## 5. Asset loading & caching (marked CRITICAL)

- **On-demand:** an image downloads only when first shown — not all upfront.
- **Two-tier cache** (`AssetService`):
  - **Memory** (Dictionary) — instant reuse this session; lost on close.
  - **Disk** (IndexedDB via `persistentDataPath`) — survives reloads; per-browser.
- **Flow:** check memory → check disk → download, then save into both.
- **In-flight de-dupe:** the same url requested twice at once shares ONE download.

## 6. WebGL / IndexedDB limitations (required explanation)

- `persistentDataPath` isn't a real disk in a browser — it's **IndexedDB**, flushed lazily → a copy may be lost if the tab closes the instant after a download.
- **Per-browser + per-site** — not shared across browsers/devices → a new browser re-downloads.
- **Quota limits;** the browser can **evict** under low-disk pressure; the user can clear it; **incognito** wipes on close; some browsers clear storage for sites unvisited for a while.
- **Memory ceiling** in WebGL — too many big textures can run the tab out of memory → needs eviction at scale.
- **No background threads** — all downloads on one thread → caching is what keeps it smooth.

## 7. Scalability thinking (feeds Task 2's required section too)

- **Data splits two ways:** *shared* (catalog + images — one copy for everyone, CDN-served, doesn't grow with users) vs *per-kid* (each kid loads only their own books via `/books/{kidId}`).
- **8000 kids:** shared art is one cached copy for all; each kid pulls only their slice; recipes are tiny text.
- **50,000 images:** IndexedDB is a **cache (fridge)**, not the **warehouse (cloud/CDN)**. Only the recently-used subset is cached; evicted items simply re-download. Add an **LRU cap** so we never blow the quota.
- **Redesign at scale:** fetch only `/books/{kidId}`; **paginate**; add an **index / search service** for discovery; rely on **CDN + browser cache** for images.
- Analogy: IndexedDB = your **fridge** (what you're using now, limited, old stuff tossed); cloud/CDN = the **grocery store** (has everything, always restockable). Never fit the store in the fridge.

## 8. Key decisions & challenges

- **REST over the SDK** (the WebGL blocker).
- **Fresh-for-data, cached-for-assets** — cache-bust the book list (always current); cache the immutable images.
- **`coverBase64`** to stay off paid Storage.
- **Per-kid data with a single `demo` id** — no login to build, but structured to scale.
- **Free Spark plan; no Cloud Functions** (see §10).

## 9. Use of AI tools

See [ai-usage-log.md](ai-usage-log.md).

## 10. Cost

Entire app runs on Firebase's **free (Spark) plan** — Realtime DB free tier, images on a free host/Hosting, covers as base64, the WebGL build on Firebase Hosting. **No credit card, no Cloud Functions.**
